intro: Every day, the whole country makes, buys and sells an enormous amount of stuff. Bakers bake. Truckers drive. Nurses care for patients. Farmers in Illinois load soybeans onto ships bound for the far side of the world. In this unit you zoom out from one store or one family to the whole nation and the whole world.

You will learn how economists measure the size of the economy with GDP. You will see why prices rise, who counts as unemployed, and what taxes pay for. You will meet the Federal Reserve. Then you will follow goods and money across borders, from tariffs and exchange rates to the supply chain behind one phone.

By the end, you will be able to read a news story about jobs, prices or trade and explain it with numbers. You will be able to name the trade-offs in a tax, a tariff or a Fed decision. And you will have the economic way of thinking to take with you.
bigQuestion: How do we measure a whole nation's economy, and how does it connect to the rest of the world?

Which part of the business cycle is the low point?
test.why: The trough is the bottom, before growth starts again.

test.q: A college student is not working and not looking for work. How is she counted?
test.why: People not working and not looking are outside the labor force.

test.q: Which of these is fiscal policy?
choices: The Fed lowers its key interest rate.
A bank raises its loan rate.
Congress passes a law to cut income taxes.
test.why: Spending and tax choices by Congress and the President are fiscal policy.

test.q: Prices are rising fast. What would the Fed most likely do?
test.why: Higher rates slow borrowing and spending, which cools inflation.

test.q: A tax takes 2% from a poor family's income and 1% from a rich family's income. What kind is it?
test.why: It takes a larger share from the lower income, so it is regressive.

test.q: The government spends $6 trillion and collects $5 trillion in a year (example numbers). What is the result?
choices: An $11 trillion debt for that year

test.q: Country A gives up 2 bikes per car. Country B gives up 5 bikes per car. Who should make cars?
test.why: Country A has the lower opportunity cost for cars.

test.q: A 15% tariff is placed on an imported $200 bike (example numbers). What is the tariff?
At 1 dollar = 20 pesos (example rate), how many pesos do you get for $50?
A weaker dollar is most likely good news for whom?
choices: An American planning a trip to Europe
An Illinois farmer selling soybeans abroad
A U.S. store selling imported shoes
A U.S. family buying a foreign car
test.why: A weaker dollar makes U.S. exports cheaper for foreign buyers.

test.q: A country has GDP of $1,200 billion and 30 million people (example numbers). What is GDP per person?

write.prompt: Your town wants to put a 20% tariff on imported bikes to protect a local bike factory. An imported bike costs $250 (example price). Figure out the tariff and the new price. Then argue whether the town should do it. Name who gains, who pays, and the opportunity cost.
tips: Show the math: 20% of $250 and the new price.
Name at least one group that gains and one that loses.
Say what else buyers could do with the extra money they pay.
Think about what other countries might do in response.
End with your choice and the main trade-off behind it.

title: The Nation and the World

chapters.title: Government, Taxes and the Whole Economy
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we tell if the whole economy is doing well, and who helps keep it steady?

story.title: Grandma and the Nickel Candy Bar
story.kicker: A candy bar once cost about a nickel. Does that mean Grandma was richer than we are?
paragraphs: Maya's grandmother likes to tell a story. When she was a girl around 1950, a candy bar cost about a nickel. She could walk to the corner store with a dime and buy two. Maya looked at the price tag at the gas station. The same kind of bar cost well over a dollar. Maya's first thought was simple. Grandma had it easy.

Then Maya asked a second question. How much money did people earn back then? Grandma laughed. Her father worked in a Chicago factory. His pay looked tiny next to what Maya's mom earns today. A nickel was not small change to him. Prices were lower, but paychecks were lower too.

Maya's teacher said economists have a name for this. When prices across the whole economy rise over time, that is inflation. To compare two years fairly, you cannot just compare prices. You must compare prices with what people earn. You also have to ask what money can buy, like cars, phones and medicine that did not exist in 1950.

This chapter zooms out from one store to the whole country. You will learn how we measure everything the country makes. You will see how prices, jobs and taxes fit together. You will also meet the Federal Reserve, which watches prices and jobs across the nation. By the end, you can answer Maya's question yourself.
story.think: Was Grandma richer or poorer than us? What two things would you need to know to decide?

lessons.title: GDP: The Size of the Economy
lessons.mainIdea: GDP is the total value of all final goods and services made in a country in one year.
reading: Picture a tiny island with one bakery and one bike shop. In one year the bakery sells 1,000 loaves at $3 each (example prices). That is $3,000. The bike shop sells 20 bikes at $200 each. That is $4,000. Add them up. The island made $7,000 worth of goods that year.

That total is the island's gross domestic product, or GDP. GDP is the market value of all final goods and services made inside a country in one year. Final means sold to the last user. We count the bread, not the flour the baker bought. Counting the flour too would count it twice.

The United States works the same way, just much bigger. Economists add up spending on houses, haircuts, trucks, doctor visits and much more. The Bureau of Economic Analysis, a federal agency, measures U.S. GDP. A bigger GDP usually means more goods, more services and more jobs.

words.d: the market value of all final goods and services made inside a country in one year
a good sold to the person who will use it, not used to make something else

look.title: Who Buys What the U.S. Makes
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, NIPA Table 1.1.10, 2023, rounded
look.prompt: Which group buys the most? Why might net exports be a negative number?

check.q: An island sells 500 hats at $10 each and 100 coats at $50 each (example prices). What is its GDP?
Why is the flour a baker buys not counted separately in GDP?
choices: Flour is too cheap to count.
It is already inside the price of the bread.
Flour is made on farms, not in cities.
check.why: GDP counts only final goods so nothing is counted twice.

check.q: Which agency measures U.S. GDP?
check.why: The Bureau of Economic Analysis, part of the Commerce Department, measures GDP.

lessons.title: Growth, Recession and the Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: The economy grows most years, but sometimes it shrinks for a while; that pattern is called the business cycle.
reading: Think of a town where factories hire more workers each year. Stores are busy. People buy new cars. This is growth. If GDP is $100 billion one year and $103 billion the next (example numbers), it grew by $3 billion. That is 3% growth.

Sometimes spending slows. Stores sell less, so they order less from factories. Factories cut hours and lay off workers. Those workers spend less, and the slowdown spreads. A widespread drop in economic activity that lasts more than a few months is called a recession.

Over many years, the economy moves up and down in waves. Economists call this the business cycle. It has an expansion, when things grow, then a peak, then a contraction, and then a low point called a trough. After the trough, growth starts again. A common mistake is thinking every dip is a recession. A short, small wobble usually is not.

words.d: a widespread drop in economic activity that lasts more than a few months
the rise and fall of economic activity over time: expansion, peak, contraction and trough
the part of the business cycle when the economy grows

look.title: A Town Slows Down
look.text: A furniture factory in a small Illinois town loses orders. It cuts 200 jobs. The laid-off workers eat out less. The diner cuts a cook. The car dealer sells fewer cars.
look.prompt: Trace the chain. How can one factory's bad year spread to other businesses?

check.q: GDP goes from $200 billion to $210 billion (example numbers). What is the growth rate?
check.why: $10 billion / $200 billion = 0.05, which is 5%.

check.q: What comes right after the peak in the business cycle?
check.why: After the top, or peak, activity falls. That falling part is the contraction.

check.q: Which event best signals a recession?
choices: One store closes for a week.
Spending, jobs and output fall across many industries for months.
check.why: A recession is broad and lasts more than a few months.

lessons.title: Real GDP versus Nominal GDP
lessons.mainIdea: Real GDP removes the effect of rising prices, so it shows whether we really made more.
reading: Go back to the island. Last year it made 1,000 loaves at $3. This year it made the same 1,000 loaves, but the price rose to $4 (example prices). GDP in dollars went from $3,000 to $4,000. Did the island make more bread? No. It made the same bread. Only the price changed.

GDP measured in current prices is called nominal GDP. It can rise just because prices rose. Real GDP uses the prices of one fixed year for every year. Using last year's $3 price, this year's real GDP is still $3,000. Real GDP shows the true change in how much was made.
When news reports say the economy grew 2%, they almost always mean real GDP. Mixing the two is a common mistake. If nominal GDP rose 5% and prices rose 3%, real output grew only about 2%.

words.d: GDP measured in the prices of the same year the goods were made
GDP measured in the prices of one fixed year, so rising prices are taken out

look.title: One Island, Two Years
look.prompt: Did nominal GDP rise? Did real GDP rise? Explain.

check.q: Nominal GDP rose 6%. Prices rose 4%. About how much did real GDP grow?
check.why: Real growth is about nominal growth minus price growth: 6% - 4% = 2%.

check.q: A country makes the same goods as last year, but prices doubled. What happened to real GDP?
check.why: Real GDP uses fixed prices, so the same goods give the same real GDP.

check.q: Why do economists prefer real GDP to compare years?
choices: It shows changes in how much was made, not just price changes.
It is always a bigger number.
It is measured by the Fed.
check.why: Real GDP takes out inflation, so it tracks real output.

lessons.title: Inflation and the Dollar
lessons.mainIdea: Inflation is a rise in the general level of prices, and it means each dollar buys less.
reading: Imagine a snack basket: a sandwich, an apple and a juice. Last year it cost $10. This year the same basket costs $10.50 (example prices). Prices rose $0.50 on $10. That is 5%. When prices across the economy go up like this, it is called inflation.

Inflation shrinks what a dollar can buy. That buying power is called purchasing power. If your allowance stays at $10 but the basket costs $10.50, you can no longer buy the whole basket. Your dollars did not change. What they can buy did.

Inflation happens for different reasons. Sometimes people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can make, so prices get pushed up. Sometimes costs like fuel jump, and businesses pass them on. The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of about 2% a year over time. A little inflation is normal. Fast inflation makes planning hard.

words.d: a rise in the general level of prices across the economy over time
how much a set amount of money can buy

look.title: The Candy Bar Question
look.text: Suppose a candy bar cost $0.05 and a worker earned $1.00 an hour (example numbers). Today suppose the bar costs $1.50 and a worker earns $15.00 an hour (example numbers).
look.prompt: How many candy bars could each worker buy with one hour of pay? Who is better off in candy bars?

check.q: A basket rises from $20 to $21 (example prices). What is the inflation rate?
Your pay stays the same while prices rise 4%. What happens to your purchasing power?
check.why: The same dollars buy fewer goods, so purchasing power falls.

check.q: About what inflation rate does the Federal Reserve aim for over time?
check.why: The Fed's stated goal is inflation of 2% over the longer run.

lessons.title: How Prices Are Measured
lessons.mainIdea: The Consumer Price Index tracks the cost of a fixed basket of things households buy.
reading: No one can check every price in the country. So the Bureau of Labor Statistics, or BLS, uses a sample. Each month it checks prices on a large basket of goods and services, like food, rent, gas, clothes and doctor visits. The result is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI.

The CPI starts from a base period set to 100. Suppose the basket's index is 100 in the base year and 110 later (example numbers). Prices rose 10% since the base. To find inflation between any two years, use percent change. From 110 to 121 is a rise of 11. Divide 11 by 110. That is 10%.

The CPI is not perfect. People change what they buy when prices change. New products appear. Quality gets better. Still, the CPI is the most used price measure. Governments use it to adjust things like Social Security payments so they keep up with prices.

words.d: a measure of the average change in prices paid by city households for a fixed basket of goods and services
the starting year for an index, set equal to 100

look.title: An Example Price Index
look.cite: Made-up example; the real CPI is published by the BLS
look.prompt: Between which two years did prices rise the most?

check.q: A price index goes from 100 to 108. By what percent did prices rise?
Which agency publishes the CPI?
check.why: The BLS, in the Labor Department, collects prices and publishes the CPI.

check.q: An index goes from 150 to 165. What is the percent change?

lessons.title: Who Counts as Unemployed
lessons.mainIdea: A person is unemployed only if they have no job, can work, and are looking for work.
reading: Picture a street with 10 adults. Six have jobs. Two have no job and are sending out applications. One is retired. One is a full-time college student who is not looking for work. Who is unemployed? Only the two who are looking.

The labor force is everyone who is working or looking for work. On this street, that is 6 + 2 = 8 people. The unemployment rate is the unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100. Here that is 2 / 8 x 100 = 25%. The retiree and the student are not in the labor force at all.

A common mistake is dividing by all adults. That would give 2 / 10 = 20%, which is wrong. The BLS finds the real rate each month with a large survey of households. The rate was about 25% in the worst year of the Great Depression and about 10% in late 2009.

words.d: all people who have a job or are actively looking for one
the unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100
having no job, being able to work, and actively looking for work

look.title: U.S. Unemployment Rate, Selected Times
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey; 1933 is a historical estimate
look.prompt: Which of these times was worst for jobs? Which was best?

check.q: A town has 90 people working and 10 looking for work. What is the unemployment rate?
A retired teacher is not looking for work. How is she counted?
check.why: She is not working and not looking, so she is outside the labor force.

check.q: A town has 45 employed, 5 unemployed and 50 retired people. What is the unemployment rate?
check.why: Labor force = 45 + 5 = 50. 5 / 50 x 100 = 10%. Retirees are not in it.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Governments collect money mostly through taxes on income, on sales and on property.
reading: Jordan earns $500 from a summer job. Some of it goes to income tax, a tax on what people earn. Then Jordan buys $40 of shoes. The store adds a sales tax, a tax on things you buy. At a rate of 6% (example rate), that adds $2.40. The shoes cost $42.40.

Jordan's family owns a house. Each year they pay property tax, a tax based on the value of land and buildings. Property taxes pay for much of the local public schools in Illinois, along with state money. Your town and county use them for roads, parks and police too.

Different levels of government lean on different taxes. The federal government collects mostly income and payroll taxes. States use income and sales taxes. Local governments use property taxes the most. Each tax makes something a little costlier, so every tax has trade-offs.

words.d: a tax on the money people and businesses earn
a tax added to the price of goods when you buy them
a tax based on the value of land and buildings someone owns

look.title: Where Does It Go?
look.text: Jordan's family pays an income tax, a sales tax at the mall, and a property tax on their home.
look.prompt: For each tax, guess which level of government most likely collects it: federal, state or local. Explain your guess.

check.q: A $50 jacket has a 6% sales tax (example rate). What is the total cost?
Which tax is most closely tied to funding local schools?
check.why: Local governments raise most of their own money through property taxes.

check.q: A $20 book has an 8% sales tax (example rate). How much is the tax?

lessons.title: Where Federal Money Goes
lessons.mainIdea: Most federal spending goes to a few big items: Social Security, health programs, defense and interest on debt.
reading: Imagine the federal government spends $100 (a pretend round number). Where would it go? In recent years, about $21 went to Social Security. About $26 went to health programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. About $13 went to national defense. About $13 went to interest on money the government borrowed.

That leaves about $27 for everything else. Everything else includes highways, food aid, veterans' benefits, science, national parks and much more. When the government spends more than it collects in taxes in a year, the gap is a deficit. It borrows to cover it, and the total borrowed over time is the debt.

Congress and the President decide the budget. This is called fiscal policy: choices about government spending and taxes. People disagree about how big the budget should be. Some say more spending helps people and builds roads and schools. Others say lower spending and taxes leave more for families and businesses. Both sides weigh trade-offs.

words.d: the amount by which government spending is more than tax money collected in one year
the total amount the federal government owes from past borrowing
choices by Congress and the President about government spending and taxes

look.title: Federal Spending per $100 (Rounded)
look.cite: Congressional Budget Office, The Federal Budget in Fiscal Year 2024, rounded
look.prompt: About what share goes to the two largest items together?

check.q: The government collects $4 trillion and spends $5 trillion in a year (example numbers). What is the deficit?
check.why: Deficit = spending minus taxes collected: $5 - $4 = $1 trillion.

check.q: Who makes fiscal policy?
check.why: Fiscal policy is about government spending and taxes, set by Congress and the President.

check.q: What is the difference between the deficit and the debt?
choices: The debt is one year's gap; the deficit is the total.
The deficit is money owed to other countries only.
The deficit is one year's gap; the debt is the total owed from many years.
check.why: Each year's deficit adds to the running total, the debt.

lessons.title: Who Pays What Share
lessons.mainIdea: A tax can take a bigger share, the same share or a smaller share of income as income rises.
reading: Two neighbors each buy $1,000 of goods and pay a 5% sales tax (example rate). Both pay $50. One neighbor earns $20,000 a year. The other earns $100,000. For the first, $50 is 0.25% of income. For the second, it is 0.05%. The same tax takes a bigger share from the lower income.

A tax that takes a larger share from lower incomes is called regressive. A tax that takes a larger share from higher incomes is progressive. The U.S. federal income tax is progressive: rates rise in steps as income rises. A tax that takes the same share from everyone is proportional, sometimes called a flat tax.

People argue about which kind is fairest. Some say those who earn more can afford to pay a larger share. Others say everyone should pay the same share, and that high rates discourage work and investment. Economists study how each design affects work, saving and fairness.

words.d: a tax that takes a larger share of income as income rises
a tax that takes a larger share of income from people with lower incomes
a tax that takes the same share of income from everyone

look.title: Test the Tax
look.text: A town charges everyone 3% of their income (example rate). Ana earns $30,000. Ben earns $90,000.
look.prompt: How much does each pay? What share of income does each pay? Which kind of tax is this?

check.q: A tax takes 10% from a $20,000 income and 25% from a $200,000 income. What kind is it?
check.why: The share rises as income rises, which makes it progressive.

check.q: Everyone pays 4% of income (example rate). How much does someone earning $50,000 pay?
check.why: 0.04 x $50,000 = $2,000. A same-share tax is proportional.

check.q: Why is a sales tax on food often called regressive?
choices: The rate goes up for poor families.
Lower-income families spend a bigger share of income on food.
It is collected by the Fed.
check.why: The rate is the same, but it takes a larger share of a smaller income.

lessons.title: The Federal Reserve
lessons.mainIdea: The Federal Reserve watches prices and jobs and sets a key interest rate to keep the economy steady.
reading: Think of the economy like a car on a long road. Too fast, and prices rise too quickly. Too slow, and people lose jobs. The Federal Reserve, often called the Fed, is the nation's central bank. Congress created it with the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.

Congress gave the Fed two main goals, often called the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices. The Fed has a board in Washington, D.C., and twelve regional Reserve Banks. One is the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, which serves Illinois and nearby states.

The Fed's main tool is a key interest rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans. When the Fed raises it, loans for cars, homes and businesses tend to cost more, so spending slows and inflation can cool. When the Fed lowers it, borrowing gets cheaper and spending can pick up. This is monetary policy. It is separate from fiscal policy, which is spending and taxes.

words.d: the central bank of the United States
actions by the Federal Reserve that change interest rates and the amount of money and credit
the Fed's two goals set by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices

look.title: What Should the Fed Do?
look.text: Prices have been rising about 6% a year (example numbers). Stores are packed and nearly everyone who wants a job has one.
look.prompt: Should the Fed raise or lower its key interest rate? Explain what that would do to borrowing and spending.

check.q: Inflation is well above 2% and rising. What would the Fed most likely do?
check.why: Higher rates make borrowing costlier, which slows spending and cools inflation.

check.q: What are the Fed's two main goals?
choices: A balanced budget and more exports
High stock prices and a strong dollar
check.why: Congress gave the Fed a dual mandate: jobs and stable prices.

check.q: How many regional Reserve Banks does the Fed have?
check.why: The Fed has twelve Reserve Banks, including one in Chicago.

review.q: A country makes 100 cars at $20,000 each and nothing else (example prices). What is its GDP?
Which is the main difference between real and nominal GDP?
choices: Real GDP takes out the effect of price changes.
review.why: Real GDP uses fixed prices, so it shows changes in output only.

review.q: A labor force has 200 people and 12 are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
A snack basket costs $40, then $42 (example prices). What is the inflation rate?
Which is an example of monetary policy?
choices: A state raises its sales tax.
The Fed raises its key interest rate.
review.why: Monetary policy is set by the Fed; tax and spending choices are fiscal policy.

review.q: A tax takes the same 5% share from every income. What kind is it?
review.why: The same share at every income is a proportional tax.

review.q: Output, jobs and spending fall across the country for many months. What is this called?
review.why: A long, widespread drop in activity is a recession.

review.q: Grandma paid $0.05 for a candy bar and earned $1.00 an hour. You pay $1.00 and earn $20.00 an hour (example numbers). How many bars does one hour of work buy?
review.why: $1.00 / $0.05 = 20 and $20.00 / $1.00 = 20, so an hour buys the same number of bars.

chapters.title: Global Trade and Development
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do countries trade, and why are some countries richer than others?

story.title: One Phone, Many Countries
story.kicker: The phone in your pocket has traveled farther than most people do in a year.
paragraphs: Luis got a new phone for his birthday. On the back, in tiny letters, it said it was designed in one country and assembled in another. Luis bought it at a store in Chicago. He wondered how many countries had touched this one small thing before it reached his hand.

His older sister looked it up. The design and software work happened in one place. The chips came from factories in other countries. Some of the glass, the battery and the metals came from still other places. The parts met in a large factory, where workers put the phone together. Then ships and planes carried it across the ocean.

Luis asked why one country did not just make the whole thing. His sister had an answer. Each place does the part it does best, at the lowest cost for what it gives up. Trading lets everyone get more than they could make alone. But trade also brings hard questions about jobs, prices and fairness.

This chapter follows goods and money across borders. You will learn why countries trade, what tariffs do, and how one currency is traded for another. You will see why some countries grow richer. You will also see how Chicago became a place where the world's trade meets.
story.think: Name one thing you own that was probably made in another country. Why might it have been made there?

lessons.title: Imports and Exports
lessons.mainIdea: An export is something sold to another country; an import is something bought from another country.
reading: An Illinois farmer grows soybeans. A buyer in another country purchases a shipload. For the United States, those soybeans are an export, a good or service sold to people in another country. Illinois is one of the top soybean-growing states, so soybeans are a big Illinois export.

Now think of a banana at a Chicago grocery. Bananas grow in warm places, so most of ours come from other countries. For the United States, that banana is an import, a good or service bought from another country. Services count too. When a tourist from abroad stays in a Chicago hotel, that is a U.S. service export.

Every import for one country is an export for another. Trade happens because people want goods they cannot make well at home, or cannot make as cheaply. The U.S. both imports and exports trillions of dollars of goods and services each year.

words.d: a good or service made in one country and sold to buyers in another country
a good or service bought from another country

look.title: Import or Export?
look.text: A Chicago company sells tractors to Brazil. A family in Peoria buys a TV made in Mexico. A visitor from Japan buys a ticket to a Cubs game.
look.prompt: For the United States, label each one an import or an export. Explain how you decided.

check.q: A company in Illinois sells corn to Japan. For the U.S., this is:
check.why: Goods sold to buyers in another country are exports.

check.q: A store in Chicago buys coffee grown in Colombia. For the U.S., the coffee is:
check.why: Goods bought from another country are imports.

check.q: A tourist from France pays for a Chicago hotel room. For the U.S., this is:
check.why: Selling a service to a foreign buyer counts as an export, even inside the U.S.

lessons.title: The Trade Balance
lessons.mainIdea: The trade balance is exports minus imports; a negative balance is a trade deficit.
reading: Picture a small country that sells $50 billion of goods to the world and buys $70 billion (example numbers). Its trade balance is exports minus imports: $50 billion - $70 billion = -$20 billion. When the balance is negative, the country has a trade deficit. When it is positive, it has a trade surplus.

The United States has run a trade deficit for many years. That means Americans buy more from other countries than they sell to them. In GDP, this shows up as net exports, the NX in C + I + G + NX. A negative NX pulls measured GDP down a little.

A common mistake is to think a trade deficit is like losing a game. It is not that simple. Buyers still got goods they wanted in return for their money, and money spent abroad often comes back as investment. Economists disagree about when a deficit is a worry. Some point to lost factory jobs. Others say it reflects strong spending and foreign investment.

words.d: the value of a country's exports minus the value of its imports
when a country imports more than it exports
when a country exports more than it imports

look.title: Example Country's Trade
look.prompt: Find the total trade balance. Is it a deficit or a surplus?

check.q: A country exports $80 billion and imports $60 billion (example numbers). What is its trade balance?
check.why: $80 - $60 = +$20 billion. Positive means a surplus.

check.q: Using the table, what is the example country's total trade balance?
In the GDP formula C + I + G + NX, what does NX stand for?
check.why: NX is net exports, the trade balance.

lessons.title: Comparative Advantage
lessons.mainIdea: Two countries both gain when each makes what it gives up the least to make, then trades.
reading: Imagine two countries, Northland and Southland. In a day, a Northland worker can make 6 shirts or 3 radios. A Southland worker can make 2 shirts or 2 radios (example numbers). Northland is better at both. Does trade still help? Yes. Look at what each gives up.

In Northland, 1 radio costs 2 shirts, because making it means giving up 2 shirts. In Southland, 1 radio costs only 1 shirt. So Southland has the lower opportunity cost for radios. For shirts, Northland gives up half a radio per shirt, while Southland gives up a whole radio. Northland has the lower cost for shirts.

A comparative advantage means making a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else. Northland should make shirts and Southland radios. If they trade at, say, 1.5 shirts for 1 radio, both get radios or shirts more cheaply than making them at home. A common mistake is to think only the country that is better at everything should make anything.

words.d: being able to make a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else
being able to make more of a good than someone else with the same resources
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: Adam Smith on Buying Instead of Making
look.text: It is the maxim of every prudent master of a family, never to attempt to make at home what it will cost him more to make than to buy.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 2, 1776
look.prompt: How does a family's choice to buy shoes instead of making them match the idea of comparative advantage?

check.q: In one day, Ana can bake 10 pies or 5 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of 1 cake?
check.why: 10 pies / 5 cakes = 2 pies given up for each cake.

check.q: Country A gives up 3 apples per orange. Country B gives up 1 apple per orange. Who has the comparative advantage in oranges?
check.why: Country B gives up less (1 apple) for each orange.

check.q: Northland is better at making both shirts and radios. Can trade still help both countries?
choices: No, trade only helps the weaker country.
Yes, if each makes the good with the lower opportunity cost.
Only if both have the same money.
check.why: Gains come from comparative advantage, not absolute advantage.

lessons.title: Tariffs and Who Pays
lessons.mainIdea: A tariff is a tax on imports; much of its cost usually shows up in higher prices for buyers at home.
reading: A bike made in another country sells in the U.S. for $200 (example price). The government puts a 25% tariff on imported bikes. A tariff is a tax on imports. It is paid to the U.S. government by the company that brings the bike in. That is $50 per bike.

Who really bears that cost? The importer may raise the price toward $250. Then American buyers pay more. Some of the cost may be absorbed by the foreign maker or the store. Studies of recent U.S. tariffs found that much of the cost was passed to U.S. buyers. A common mistake is to think the foreign country simply pays the tax.

Tariffs have trade-offs. They can protect jobs at American bike makers, who now face less competition. They can raise money for the government. But buyers pay higher prices, and other countries may answer with tariffs on U.S. exports, such as Illinois soybeans. Economists debate when, if ever, the protection is worth the cost.

words.d: a tax on goods brought into a country from another country
using tariffs or other limits on imports to shield home businesses from foreign competition

look.title: A Tariff on Steel
look.text: The U.S. puts a tariff on imported steel. A steel mill in Indiana hires 100 more workers. A Chicago company that makes car parts from steel now pays more for its steel.
look.prompt: Who gains and who loses from this tariff? Name at least two of each.

check.q: An imported $40 toy has a 10% tariff (example numbers). How much is the tariff?
Who sends tariff money to the U.S. government?
choices: The company that brings the goods into the U.S.
Each store's customers directly at the register
check.why: U.S. importers pay the tariff; they often pass much of it on in higher prices.

check.q: Another country answers a U.S. tariff with a tariff on U.S. soybeans. Who is most likely hurt?
check.why: A tariff on U.S. soybeans makes them costlier abroad, so farmers sell less.

lessons.title: Exchange Rates on a Trip
lessons.mainIdea: An exchange rate is the price of one country's money in another country's money.
reading: Sofia's family visits Mexico. In Mexico, prices are in pesos, not dollars. At the bank, suppose 1 U.S. dollar trades for 20 pesos (example rate). That number is the exchange rate, the price of one currency in terms of another. Currency is simply a country's money.

Sofia sees a T-shirt for 300 pesos. How many dollars is that? Divide by the rate: 300 / 20 = $15. She changes $100 at the bank. She gets 100 x 20 = 2,000 pesos. Always ask which way the rate goes. Multiply dollars by 20 to get pesos. Divide pesos by 20 to get dollars.

Exchange rates change every day. Traders buy and sell currencies, so the price moves with supply and demand. If more people want dollars, the dollar's price rises. That is why a trip can cost more one year and less the next, even when prices in the other country stay the same.

words.d: the price of one country's money in terms of another country's money
the kind of money used in a country, like the dollar, the peso or the euro

look.title: A Trip Budget in Pesos
look.prompt: Change each cost to dollars. What does the whole list cost in dollars?

check.q: At 1 dollar = 20 pesos (example rate), how many dollars is a 500-peso meal?
At 1 dollar = 0.9 euros (example rate), how many euros do you get for $200?
What mostly makes exchange rates change from day to day?
choices: Supply and demand for each currency
A fixed law set once a year
The number of banks in a city
check.why: Currencies are traded like goods, so their prices move with supply and demand.

lessons.title: A Strong or a Weak Dollar
lessons.mainIdea: When the dollar gets stronger, imports and trips abroad get cheaper for Americans, and U.S. exports cost more for others.
reading: Say the rate moves from 1 dollar = 20 pesos to 1 dollar = 25 pesos (example rates). Each dollar now buys more pesos. The dollar has become stronger. Sofia's 300-peso T-shirt now costs 300 / 25 = $12 instead of $15. Trips and imports from Mexico got cheaper for Americans.

Now flip it. A Mexican family wants to buy a U.S. product that costs $100. At 20 pesos per dollar, that is 2,000 pesos. At 25, it is 2,500 pesos. The strong dollar made U.S. goods more expensive for them. So a strong dollar tends to help U.S. shoppers and travelers but can hurt U.S. exporters.

A weaker dollar does the opposite. U.S. exports get cheaper for other countries, so farmers and factories may sell more abroad. But imports and foreign trips cost Americans more. A common mistake is to think a strong dollar is simply good. Whether it helps depends on whether you are buying from abroad or selling to it.

words.d: when a currency becomes worth more compared with another currency
when a currency becomes worth less compared with another currency

look.title: Who Cheers?
look.text: The dollar gets much weaker against the euro. Three people read the news: an Illinois farmer who sells corn to Europe, a family planning a trip to Italy, and a store that sells German cars.
look.prompt: Who is happy about the weaker dollar and who is not? Explain for each.

check.q: The rate goes from 1 dollar = 20 pesos to 1 dollar = 25 pesos. The dollar has:
check.why: Each dollar buys more pesos, so it rose in value.

check.q: A weaker dollar most likely helps which group?
check.why: A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper for foreign buyers.

check.q: At 1 dollar = 25 pesos (example rate), how many pesos does a $100 U.S. item cost?

lessons.title: Supply Chains: One Phone
lessons.mainIdea: A supply chain is every step and place that goods pass through, from raw materials to the buyer.
reading: Follow a phone backward. Before the store, it rode in a truck. Before that, a ship or plane. Before that, a factory put it together. Before that, other factories made the chips, the screen and the battery. Before that, mines dug up metals. All these steps together make a supply chain.

Companies spread the steps across countries to lower costs and use special skills. One place may have expert chip makers. Another may have many trained assembly workers. Another may have the mines. Using each place for what it does best is comparative advantage at work. Linking the world's economies this way is called globalization.

Long supply chains have a weak spot. If one step stops, everything waits. During the COVID-19 pandemic, closed factories and crowded ports delayed many goods, and some prices rose. Since then, some companies have moved steps closer to home or found more than one supplier. That can add safety but also add cost.

words.d: all the steps, people and places that turn raw materials into a product and get it to the buyer
the growing links among the world's economies through trade, travel, money and ideas

look.title: One Broken Link
look.text: A fire shuts down the only factory that makes a small chip used in a popular car. The car maker has no other supplier.
look.prompt: Trace what happens next to the car factory, its workers, car dealers and car prices.

check.q: Which is the best example of a supply chain step?
choices: A mine digs up metal later used in a phone battery.
A student reads a phone's manual.
A family pays its phone bill.
A teacher collects phones in class.
check.why: A supply chain covers the steps that make and deliver the product.

check.q: Why do companies spread phone-making steps across many countries?
choices: Because laws require at least five countries
To use each place's skills and lower costs
check.why: Each step goes where it can be done at lower cost, an idea based on comparative advantage.

check.q: What is one risk of a long supply chain?
choices: Goods can only be sold in one country.
One stopped step can delay the whole product.
check.why: Every step depends on the one before it.

lessons.title: Why Some Countries Are Richer
lessons.mainIdea: Countries grow richer mostly by making more per worker, helped by education, health, good institutions and trade.
reading: Picture two farms. On one, a family digs by hand and grows enough to eat. On the other, a trained farmer uses a tractor, good seed and weather data, and grows food for hundreds of people. The second farm has much higher productivity: more output per worker per hour.

Productivity is the main reason some countries are richer. It grows with human capital, the skills and health of workers, and with physical capital, like tools, machines and roads. It also grows with new technology. Economists often compare countries using GDP per person, which is GDP divided by population.

Institutions matter too. Institutions are the rules of the game: fair courts, protected property, honest government and stable money. When people trust that they can keep what they earn, they build and invest. Trade helps by opening bigger markets and new ideas. No single recipe fits every country, and economists still debate which steps matter most.

words.d: the amount of goods and services made per worker or per hour of work
the skills, knowledge and health that make workers productive
a country's GDP divided by its population

look.title: GDP per Person: Two Example Countries
look.prompt: Find GDP per person for each. Which country has more GDP but less per person?

check.q: A country has GDP of $800 billion and 40 million people (example numbers). What is GDP per person?
A country spends more on schools and job training. Which part of growth does this build?
check.why: Education builds workers' skills, which is human capital.

check.q: Why do fair courts and protected property help a country grow?
choices: People invest when they trust they can keep what they build.
check.why: Good institutions give people reasons to save, invest and start businesses.

lessons.title: Chicago: Where Trade Meets
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago grew as a trade hub because railroads, waterways, farms and markets all met there.
reading: Look at a map of the Midwest. Chicago sits where the Great Lakes come close to rivers that lead to the Mississippi. In the 1800s, canals and then railroads linked the city to farms to the west and cities to the east. Grain, lumber and livestock poured in. Chicago grew fast.

In 1848, traders founded the Chicago Board of Trade. It became a place to buy and sell grain, and later contracts for grain to be delivered in the future. Farmers and buyers used it to set prices and manage risk. It is now part of CME Group, and its prices are watched around the world.

Today Chicago is still a crossroads. Many major railroads meet there, and O'Hare Airport handles large amounts of air cargo. Illinois farms send soybeans and corn abroad, and Illinois factories export machinery. When world trade rises or falls, Chicago feels it quickly.

words.d: a place where many routes meet, so goods are gathered, traded and shipped
an agreement to buy or sell something at a set price on a later date

look.title: Why Here?
look.text: In the 1850s, a farmer in Iowa wants to sell wheat to a baker in New York. A railroad runs from Iowa to Chicago, and ships and trains run from Chicago to the East.
look.prompt: Explain why the wheat would pass through Chicago and how that helped the city grow.

check.q: In what year was the Chicago Board of Trade founded?
check.why: Traders founded the Chicago Board of Trade in 1848.

check.q: What helped make Chicago a trade hub in the 1800s?
choices: A law making it the capital
Waterways and railroads linking farms to eastern cities
check.why: Transport links brought farm goods through Chicago.

check.q: A farmer agrees today to sell corn next fall at a set price. What is this?
check.why: A futures contract fixes a price now for a sale later.

lessons.title: The Economic Way of Thinking
lessons.mainIdea: Economists look at choices, costs, incentives and trade-offs to understand people, markets and nations.
reading: You started this course with wants and needs. Now you can see the whole world economy. Through it all, a few ideas kept coming back. Resources are scarce, so every choice has an opportunity cost. People respond to incentives, like prices, wages and taxes.

Trade helps both sides when each does what it gives up the least to do. Markets use prices to share information. Governments set rules, collect taxes and provide some goods. The Fed tries to keep prices steady and jobs plentiful. Each step has trade-offs, and wise choices name them.

Try it on a real question. Should your town build a new park? Ask what it costs, what else that money could do, who gains, who pays, and how people's behavior might change. That set of questions is the economic way of thinking. You can use it at the store, at work and when you vote.

words.d: something that encourages people to act in a certain way, like a reward or a cost
giving up some of one thing to get more of another

look.title: David Ricardo on Free Trade
look.text: Under a system of perfectly free commerce, each country naturally devotes its capital and labour to such employments as are most beneficial to each.
look.cite: David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, Chapter 7, 1817
look.prompt: What does Ricardo think countries will do if trade is free? What might someone who disagrees say?

check.q: A city spends $2 million on a park instead of fixing roads. What is the opportunity cost?
choices: The road repairs it did not make
check.why: Opportunity cost is the next-best use given up, here the road repairs.

check.q: A store puts snacks on sale and sells twice as many. Which idea does this show?
check.why: A lower price is an incentive that changes behavior.

check.q: Which question best fits the economic way of thinking?
choices: What did we do last year?
What would a famous person choose?
Who gains, who pays, and what is given up?
check.why: Economic thinking weighs costs, benefits and trade-offs.

review.q: Illinois sells machinery to Canada. For the U.S., this is:
A country exports $30 billion and imports $45 billion (example numbers). Its trade balance is:
A worker in Country X can make 4 cups or 2 plates in a day. What is the opportunity cost of 1 plate?
A 20% tariff is placed on a $300 imported TV (example numbers). How much is the tariff?
At 1 dollar = 150 yen (example rate), how many dollars is a 3,000-yen meal?
The dollar gets stronger. What happens to the cost of a trip abroad for Americans?
review.why: Each dollar buys more foreign money, so trips cost fewer dollars.

review.q: Which change would most likely raise a country's productivity?
choices: Better schools and training for workers
review.why: More human capital lets each worker make more.

review.q: What does the U.S. government receive from a tariff?
review.why: A tariff is a tax on imports, paid by the importing company.
